name: Temperance 'Tem' Quarles
languages: Enough Spanish to ask for water, a horse and a man by name
equipment: Leather duster, canvas-colored, patched at both elbows, with a pocket sewn inside for warrants
Army revolver (Colt Single Action, 1873, bought new in Fort Worth with the Coryell County bounty), 5 rounds loaded and the hammer on an empty chamber, in a cross-draw holster
Repeating rifle (Winchester '66, brass frame, her father's), 12 rounds loaded, in a saddle scabbard
Two pairs of manacles and a length of chain
Field glasses, army surplus, one lens cracked
Saddle and tack, bedroll, slicker, canteen (2)
Riding horse: a big plain bay mare called Sunday, who does not like men
A tally book with the names of eleven men she has brought in, the dates, and the word ALIVE after each one
The poster, folded in eight, in her hatband
features: Hard Country (Frontier-Born origin: advantage on saving throws against exhaustion from heat, cold, thirst and hard travel; she needs only half the usual water one day in three; once per long rest she can shrug off a level of exhaustion gained on the trail; her packed rations last a day longer)

Quick Draw (Gunslinger: advantage on initiative rolls and on the draw in a showdown; when she rolls initiative and is not surprised she can draw a Sidearm as part of the roll; drawing and holstering a Sidearm never costs her an interaction)
Gun Hand: Steady Hand (Gunslinger: once on each of her turns, when she rolls a 1 on a damage die for a Sidearm single shot, she can reroll that die and must use the new roll)

Fan the Hammer (Gunslinger, 2nd level: when she fans a single-action revolver she can fan up to 4 rounds in one action, and the first attack is made without disadvantage; fanned shots add no ability modifier to damage)

Style: Trick Shooter (Gunslinger, 3rd level: her called shots take -2 instead of -5, and she can shoot a weapon, a rope, a lamp or a hat off a head as a called shot with no chance of hitting the person; it is how she brings them in breathing)

Paper on Him (Bounty Hunter background: sheriffs, marshals and express agents know her as someone who brings them in, and will tell her who is wanted, for what, for how much and where last seen; she knows how rewards are paid and who pays honestly; outlaws and their kin know her face too)

personality.traits: I say about one word in five that I think. I count things: cartridges, miles, the men in a room, the steps to the door. I eat standing up. When somebody tells me a man is guilty, I ask how they know.
personality.ideals: A man on a poster is a man until a judge says otherwise. I bring them in breathing, every one, and let the law do the hanging if it wants to. That way it's on the law and not on me.
personality.bonds: My sister Patience's two boys, Jody and Dan, in the orphans' home at Galveston since the fever took her and her husband in '72. The home will let them go to kin who can show a farm and a judge's order. Two thousand dollars is the farm and the order and enough over to feed them.
personality.flaws: The poster says dead or alive, and the money's the same either way, and I have caught myself thinking how much easier dead would be. I didn't used to think like that. I'm scared of what I'll do if it comes down to the boys or him.

appearance: A rangy, weathered woman of thirty-one with a long jaw, sun-creased grey eyes, and straw-colored hair cut short as a boy's under a flat black hat with a rattlesnake band. Canvas duster, man's trousers, a cross-draw holster, spurs she never uses. She moves without hurry and sits with her back to walls.
backstory: Temperance Quarles grew up on a horse ranch on the San Saba with a father who taught her to shoot, track and keep her mouth shut, and a mother who taught her to read from the Bible and the stock catalogue. When the ranch failed in '67 her father took to man-hunting for the rewards and took her with him, because she could follow a trail better than he could. He was killed in '69 by a man he had brought in alive, who came out of the Huntsville penitentiary on a pardon and found him. Tem brought that man in too, alive, and went on in the trade alone. In nine years she has brought in eleven men and never killed one, and she is known from Fort Worth to San Antonio as the woman who brings them back breathing, which some sheriffs like and some do not. Her sister Patience died of yellow fever in Galveston in 1872 and left two boys in the orphans' home there. Tem visits them twice a year. She has decided that two thousand dollars is the number at which she quits, and she has never seen a poster with that number on it until this one. She has heard of the Thale brothers; they have heard of her.
